accroche: Its planks are replaced one by one. When the last one has been changed, is it still the same ship?
contenu_vulgarise:
The ship on which Theseus returned from Crete was preserved in Athens and maintained for centuries. When a plank rotted, it was replaced; then another, then yet another. Plutarch, who reports the fact in his *Life of Theseus*, notes that the philosophers of his time already drew a question from it: once all the planks have been changed, is it still the same ship?

We smile. Then we look for the answer, and we do not find it.

## Two Answers, Both Reasonable

Saying no seems solid: nothing remains of the original material. But then, at what point did it stop being itself? At the first plank? At the fiftieth? No threshold imposes itself, and an arbitrary threshold is not an answer. It is a decision disguised as an observation.

Saying yes seems solid too: the form, the function and the continuity of use were never interrupted. But then identity depends on nothing material, which is a heavy conclusion to take on.

## Hobbes's Twist

In 1655, in the *De Corpore*, Thomas Hobbes adds a twist that makes the problem frankly insoluble. Let us imagine that a collector has gathered every plank that was removed, and assembles them in their original configuration.

Two ships now exist. The one in the harbor, which has never stopped sailing but of which not one plank is original. And the one in the shed, made exactly of Theseus's materials, but which has never been used.

Which one is the ship of Theseus? Both answers can be defended, and they cannot both be true. Hobbes draws a useful conclusion from this: “the same” covers two distinct criteria, same form, same matter, which everyday language confuses without harm, because they almost always coincide. Almost.

## Why This Concerns You

Your cells renew themselves. Your memories are rewritten at each recall. The opinions you held at twenty, you would no longer defend. Nothing that made you up twenty years ago has remained intact, and yet your loved ones, the civil registry and you yourself take it as obvious that you are the same person.

It is not obvious. It is a criterion, chosen without having been formulated. The question becomes concrete as soon as it is applied: does a contract signed thirty years ago still bind you, and in the name of what? The ship of Theseus settles nothing. It makes visible the choice we had made without seeing it.

repere.texte: In 1655, Hobbes doubles the problem: if all the removed planks are gathered, two ships exist at the same time, the one that never left the harbor, and the one made of the original planks.

carte.punch: Your cells renew themselves. Your memories are rewritten. Are you the same person?
carte.idee: The ship of Theseus: its planks are replaced one by one. Hobbes adds the trap in 1655: if the removed planks are reassembled, two ships exist. Neither is more legitimate than the other.

quiz.question: What difficulty does Hobbes add in 1655 to the problem of the ship of Theseus?
choix: He shows that no plank of the original ship could ever have been kept
He demonstrates that the question is one of language and not of metaphysics
He gathers the removed planks: two legitimate ships then exist together
He proposes to set the identity threshold at half of the planks replaced
quiz.explication: By reconstituting a second ship with the original planks, Hobbes brings out two simultaneous candidates: the one that has continuity of form and use, the one that has the matter. The two criteria, ordinarily confused because they coincide, come apart, and nothing allows us to prefer one. Setting an arbitrary threshold solves nothing: it is the very difficulty the case reveals.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who reports the riddle of the ship of Theseus in antiquity?
choix: Plutarch, in his Life of Theseus
Thomas Hobbes, in the De Corpore
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is Plutarch who reports the fact in his Life of Theseus, noting that the philosophers of his time already drew from it a question about the identity of the restored ship.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does setting a threshold, for example half of the planks replaced, not solve the problem according to the entry?
choix: Because the archives of the Athenian navy do not allow the exact number of planks to be verified
Because Plutarch explicitly forbids, in his text, setting such a threshold
Because no threshold imposes itself: an arbitrary threshold is a decision disguised as an observation
Because the ship's original planks could never be identified with certainty
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry states it directly: saying no implies finding a precise moment when the ship stops being itself, yet no threshold imposes itself, it is a decision disguised as an observation.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How is the personal example (cells, memories, opinions) comparable to the ship of Theseus, according to the entry?
choix: Because human cells, unlike the planks of a ship, never renew themselves entirely
Because nothing that made up the person twenty years ago has remained intact, and yet the person is held to be the same
Because the law imposes a precise threshold, the age of thirty, to settle the question of personal identity
Because Hobbes himself applies the ship example to personal identity in the De Corpore
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Like the ship, nothing that made up the person of twenty years ago has remained intact, neither cells nor memories nor opinions. Yet loved ones, the civil registry and the person themselves hold them to be the same.
